lectures.title: Adding Buttons & Modes to the Authentication Screen

cues.en: So let's now continue work on
that auth form here.
Back in auth.dart, we should now add some buttons
to that form and then also fine tune those text form fields.
But I'll start with the buttons.
For that here, I'll first add a sized box
to add some spacing between those inputs and the buttons
where I simply set a height of let's say 12.
And then below that sized box here,
I wanna have two buttons, which are not next to each other
but above each other instead though.
The first button will be the main button
that can be used for submitting the form.
And here I'll use an elevated button
where the child will be a text widget
where I simply wanna say "Signup."
And this can be const.
And onPressed then will be a function,
which at the moment will be empty,
but which later will make sure
that all the input values are collected
and sent to Firebase.
That's the idea behind this button.
The second button, which I wanna add below
this elevated button will be a text button here for me,
which the end should allow users to toggle
and switch between sign up and log in mode
because of course this form should be usable
to either create a new account if you don't have one
or log in with an existing account if you do have one.
And at the moment we only have email
and password inputs here,
but later we'll also add image upload.
But the image upload should only be enforced and available
if you're creating a new account.
If you're logging into an existing account,
you already have an image,
and you don't need to upload one again.
Therefore, it will be important to differentiate
between login and signup mode.
And this button here will allow users
to switch between those modes.
So therefore here we of course also have onPressed
and at the moment I'll set this to an empty function,
but we'll also have a child which displays a text widget
where we in the end say create an account
or alternatively log in with an existing account
or something like this
depending on the mode in which we currently are.
And in the end, that's also one reason
for using a stateful widget here
because now we can manage that mode as state in that widget.
Here we can add a new variable
that could be named _isLogin
controlling whether we are in login mode or not.
And we could initially set this to true,
so that login mode is our default.
And then down there at the buttons,
we could say that this button, which will allow us to switch
between those modes, either says, "Create an account"
or says "I already have an account.
"Login," something like this.
And here I wanna use a ternary expression
based on the isLogin variable we just added,
the isLogin property,
and therefore here I'm checking whether isLogin is true.
If that's the case, this button should allow us
to switch to signup mode
and will therefore say, "Create an account."
Alternatively, it will say,
"I already have an account.
"Login instead," and that's a bit long.
So therefore I'll just say, "I already have an account."
And here in this function I then of course wanna
switch my mode.
So here we can use set state
to set isLogin equal to true if it's currently false
or false if it's currently true.
And we could write it like this
and use a ternary expression here
and check if it's true, in which case
we set isLogin to false, and otherwise we set it to true.
But that's unnecessarily long.
A shorter way of setting isLogin to its opposite
is to use an exclamation mark here and then isLogin
because this exclamation mark
basically checks for the opposite
as you learned earlier in the course.
If this is true, exclamation mark true will yield false.
If isLogin is false,
exclamation mark isLogin will yield true.
That's the idea here.
So this allows us to easily switch
between these two different possible values.
And this button's text will then be updated
based on the value.
But it's not just the text of this button here,
it's also the text of this button that should be updated.
This should not be const.
Instead here I wanna say Signup if we are in signup mode,
but I want to say Login if we are in login mode.
So "Login" is my alternative text
and I'll check this isLogin property
with another ternary expression here.
And then later this will also influence
whether we're sending a request to Firebase
to create a new user or to login an existing user.
But we'll get back to that later.
So for the moment it's just about those button texts.
And if you now save this, we should see these buttons here.
And if I tap create an account here,
you see the button texts change.
If I create an account, we switch to signup mode.
If I click on "I already have an account,"
we switch to login mode instead.
Now here, I just also want to adjust the button styling,
and I could do this through my theme,
but since in this app here,
this will basically be the only place
where I'll use an elevated button.
I'll adjust the styling right here on the button
by setting style equal to elevatedButton.styleFrom
as you also learned a bit earlier in the course
or I guess way earlier in the course,
but either way.
Here we can then set the foreground color
and the background color.
And I wanna set the background color here,
and I'll set the background color
to theme of context color scheme to access the colors
of my globally available theme.
And here I'll choose primary container.
And with that I'll have this nice background here,
but with that we now added those buttons,
therefore it's now time to come back to those inputs
and make sure that those inputs get validated.
And we also then are able to extract the entered values.
So now to build this auth screen,
here in my Flutter project,
I'll add a new folder in the lib folder,
which I'll name screens to store my screen widgets in there,
and in that folder, I'll add a new auth.dart file.
The name of course is up to you,
but in there, I wanna create that auth screen widget,
which in the end will be responsible
for collecting that user input.
Now for that, in there,
we of course create a new class which I'll name AuthScreen,
and which here, extends StatefulWidget,
and I'll extend StatefulWidget here,
because I will render a form
and collect some user data through that form,
and for that, we'll have to use some features
that require a StatefulWidget.
Now, in this StatefulWidget here,
I'll add my constructor, AuthScreen,
where I accept and forward that key,
and where I add that createState method.
And then we also add this _AuthScreenState class
in addition to the AuthScreen widget class
where we extend the State object that will be connected
to the AuthScreen class,
and that will also be the case here, of course.
And in that State class here,
we have that build method as we always do,
and as we always did throughout this entire course.
With that, we can then instantiate
this _AuthScreenState class here in the createState method.
And then here in the build method,
we return our widget tree for this screen.
And here, I wanna start with a Scaffold,
because of course, I want to make sure
that we do have this nice styling
and this background color that we might want to have.
And on that scaffold here,
I'll add the backgroundColor parameter to add,
guess what, a background color to that scaffold.
And here, I'll use my Theme.of constructor function
with the context to get hold of my theme setup
or to my theme settings,
and then there, we can access the colorScheme property.
And then there, I wanna use the primary property,
so the primary color that I did in the end set up.
In addition to setting that backgroundColor here,
I'll also add the body parameter,
and then here, I wanna render the actual auth form.
Now, for that here, I'll render a Center widget
so that all the content inside
of it will take the entire width and height of the screen
and will be centered in that width and height.
And then inside of Center, I wanna have a child
that is a SingleChildScrollView
because I'm going to add a column
with multiple text inputs here,
and I wanna make sure that even if the keyboard is open,
all these inputs and buttons are always reachable.
So the therefore, I ensure
that the content will be scrollable
by wrapping SingleChildScrollView around a Column,
and that Column will then hold the actual inputs and so on.
Now on that column, I'll set mainAxisAlignment
to MainAxisAlignment.center
to again center all the content inside of this column.
And then here, we'll have a couple of children,
of course, a couple of child widgets.
Now, when it comes to those child widgets,
I wanna start with a container
to add some margin to it
with EdgeInsets
only to target the different directions individually,
to add a top margin of 30, a bottom margin of 20,
and also a left and right margin of 20.
Those values should ensure
that this container will be positioned
exactly the way I want to position it.
But what's the purpose of this container, you might wonder.
Well, the purpose is to, in the end, display an image,
so that will be the child of the container.
I'll also add a width to the container to set this
to 200 pixels to size this image appropriately.
Now, when it comes to that image,
you'll find the Chat png file attached,
and I will create a new folder in my project here,
which I'll name assets.
And in there, I'll add an images folder,
and in there, I'll store that attached chat.png file,
so that's inside of assets/images.
With that image added here, I'll also go to pubspec.yaml
because as you learned earlier in the course,
if you have some assets like an image in your project
that should be usable in your app code,
you also have to go to the pubspec.yaml file
and comment in this assets part here,
and then simply reference that asset,
so that image, for example, that should be available.
So here, the assets/images/chat.png path,
pointing at the image we added here.
With that added, we can go back to auth.dart,
and in that widget here, inside of this container,
I'll now use the Image.asset constructor function
to reference that image I just added,
which is in that assets/images/chat.png path here.
So with that, I'm effectively setting up a container
with some margin and with a fixed width
that will display this image.
And I'm simply adding this for styling reasons,
to make this app or this screen look good.
Below this container,
I then wanna have the actual authentication form.
So below this container here, I'll add a Card widget
like this, to have this nice card styling,
this nice card look.
And here on this Card, I'll also add some margin
and set this to EdgeInsets.all(20) like this
to add a margin of 20 in all directions around the card.
And then the child of this card here will be
yet another SingleChildScrollView to ensure
that the content inside of this card is scrollable
and all the content is always reachable.
And here, I'll wrap this around a Padding widget
to add some inner padding inside of that card,
so between the borders of that card,
the edges of the card, and the actual card content.
And the amount of padding is then set up
with the padding parameter,
and here, I'll set this to EdgeInsets.all(16).
And then the child of that padding will be that form,
so ultimately that authentication form
which you wanna build,
and for that, I'll use the Form widget
provided by Flutter, about which you also learned
in greater detail in an earlier course section.
And this Form will then display a Column widget,
it will contain a Column widget,
which in the end will display the individual form inputs,
so the different text fields that will be displayed.
Now for that here, on that column,
I'll set the main axis size
to MainAxisSize.min to make sure
that this column will only take as much space as needed
by its content, essentially, instead of taking as much space
as it can get and having no boundaries on the vertical axis.
And then the children of this inner column in that form,
in that card, will, as mentioned, be those input elements.
And for that here, we can for example,
add a TextFormField, which should allow users
to enter their email address.
And therefore, I wanna add a label that tells them such
by adding the decoration parameter
and adding an InputDecoration object here
to configure the decoration of this TextFormField.
And then here, we can set the labelText parameter
in that InputDecoration constructor function here
to Email Address, for example,
and this can be a const object.
Now, in addition to setting that label,
I also wanna set the keyboardType of this TextFormField
to TextInputType.emailAddress,
which as the name suggests in the end, ensures
that the soft keyboard that will be opened will be optimized
for entering email addresses, by for example,
ensuring that the at symbol is easy to reach.
In addition, I'll add another property
which we haven't used before in the course,
and that will be the autocorrect property,
which I'll set to false to turn off auto-correction,
because that can of course be super annoying
if you're entering an email address
and you're getting corrected all the time.
In addition, we can also set TextCapitalization
to TextCapitalization.none
to ensure that the email address won't get capitalized,
so that the first character
of the email address won't be uppercase,
because that can also be very annoying.
Now with that, we have a basic TextFormField,
and I'm not done with it yet.
There are still a couple of key features missing,
but I wanna see something on the screen,
and therefore, I will just copy this
to also add another TextFormField that allows users
to enter their password by adding a labelText
of Password to that next TextFormField.
And here, the keyboardType will actually be
the regular text keyboardType,
and therefore, I'll remove this.
I also will remove autocorrect and textCapitalization,
but here, since this input will be all about users entering
their password, I'll set a never,
very important parameter, on TextFormField.
I'll set the obscureText parameter to true,
which simply hides the characters as they are being entered,
so that if someone were to stand
behind the person using that app,
that person couldn't see the entered password.
Well, and with that, as mentioned,
we're absolutely not done with this form.
There's a lot missing here,
but we have these two input fields in that form,
in that card, on that AuthScreen,
and I just wanna make sure
that we're going into the right direction.
Therefore, I'll save that file, and back in main.dart,
we can now import and use that AuthScreen.
So here, I'll import from my chat_app project,
and there from the screens folder, the auth.dart file.
And with this import added here, we can then
of course go down here, and set AuthScreen as the widget
that should be displayed in our app here,
and here, we can add const.
With that, if we then run this app here,
we will be greeted by this basic authentication screen,
as mentioned, not finished, but not looking too bad.
And here, if I tap into this email address field,
you'll see that a soft keyboard opened up
that makes entering email addresses quite convenient
by giving us this at symbol here, so that we can enter
our email addresses here with great ease.
And the password field,
on the upper hand, gives us a regular keyboard,
but if I enter something here,
you see that those characters are obscured,
which of course also is great.
